{
    "id": "10-computer-use/app-readiness-probing",
    "title": "App Readiness Probing",
    "category": "10-computer-use",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Probe a launched application with an ordered, bounded check sequence and an injectable clock so downstream computer-use actions begin only once the app verifiably accepts them.",
    "body": "App Readiness Probing Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An app process being alive does not mean its UI is usable: windows take time, ports open late, and services initialize in order. Readiness probing turns “it started” into evidence — an ordered list of checks re-evaluated on a fixed schedule until every check holds within a declared budget. The probe fails loudly when the budget is spent, carrying the elapsed time and the checks that still failed. When to Use Use after launching or connecting to an application — local desktop app, remote VM, or headed service — before any scripted interaction with its UI. Do not use for continuous health monitoring of long-lived services; that is infrastructure probing, which has different lifecycle rules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Ordered readiness checks, evaluated in order each cycle | | | | Yes | Total readiness budget in seconds | | | | Yes | Delay between probe cycles | | | | No | Injectable time source for deterministic tests | Procedure 1. Define each check against an externally observable condition — listening port, window present, login prompt visible — never against process liveness alone. 2. Order checks by dependency: earlier checks must hold before later ones can be meaningful. 3. Evaluate every check each cycle in a fixed order, computing readiness as all-checks-hold. 4. Return the elapsed time at first success so startup cost is measured, not guessed. 5. On budget expiry, fail with elapsed time plus the list of still-failing checks. 6. Bind the budget to an injectable clock so probes replay identically in tests. 7. Re-measure the budget after environment changes; a budget tuned once is a stale budget. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Elapsed seconds when all checks passed, or null on timeout | | | | Checks still failing when the budget expired | | | | Number of probe cycles executed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Premature interaction | UI driven before services finished starting | Gate all scripted actions behind the readiness probe | | Liveness confusion | Process existence treated as readiness | Probe observable capabilities, not process liveness | | Unmeasured startup | Budget guessed from one machine | Record observed elapsed times and tune on evidence | | Clock coupling | Probes read the wall clock in tests | Inject the clock for deterministic replay | | Silent ti meout | Failure swallowed by the caller | Treat probe timeout as a blocking error with diagnostics | Security and Authority Boundary Probing grants no authority; it only observes. Probes must use the same authenticated session the actions will use and must not probe systems outside the automation’s declared scope. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Kubernetes documentation for liveness, readiness, and startup probes (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/). 2. Python’s socket module documentation for connectivity checks (https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Triage replaces reflex with a rule table — each source maps to a declared action class and deduplication key, repeated notifications collapse, and the output is an ordered action list. The rules are data, versioned with the corpus, and reviewable. When to Use Use when an agent or assistant monitors a desktop notification stream and must decide — by recorded policy — which notifications interrupt a task, which queue for later, and which are dropped. Give every source an explicit rule row before the stream starts; unmapped sources default to ignore, never to act. 2. Compute the deduplication key from the declared field; a missing key makes a notification non-deduplicatable and it is treated as unique. 3. Drop ignored and duplicate notifications before any action; duplicates never reach the action list. 4. Emit actions in arrival order as (source, action, key) triples so the decision trail is replayable. 5. Version the rule table with the agent configuration; triage behavior must be reproducible from the recorded rules. 6. Review dropped and duplicate counts periodically; a rule that drops everything real is a misconfiguration.
